subtype: Approach: venting in the group chat [Pitfall]
passage: Honestly, Jagdish, the group chat post was the worst idea I had all year. My best friend Minal had promised to sit with me at the quiz and then sat with the debate girls. I was furious. So I typed, "Some people say they're your friend and then disappear." No name. Just that, in the class chat. For about ten minutes it was lovely: hearts, "who is it??", someone writing "been there." Then Minal read it. Everyone knew who, because of the quiz. She left the chat and did not pick up my call. Now when I want to say sorry and explain, I can't even begin, because she thinks the whole class was laughing at her. I wanted one person to hear me, and I told forty. I'm Sharmila, and I would delete that post if I could.

qa.q: Where did Sharmila post the vague complaint?
qa.a: Sharmila posted it in the class chat.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when typing the post, and what set it off?
qa.a: Sharmila was hurt and furious because Minal promised to sit at the quiz and then sat with the debate girls.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do instead to be heard by Minal, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila could ask Minal for a private one-to-one talk and say how the quiz felt, because an honest talk needs to feel safe rather than public.

qa.q: How does the post look to Minal?
qa.a: Minal, named by everyone's guess, likely feels embarrassed and rejected, which is why Minal left the chat and ignored the call.

grounding: Hurt and angry, the student posts vague complaints in a shared chat, which brings brief sympathy but spreads the conflict, embarrasses the friend and makes an honest talk harder.

passage: Kishore, you asked why I never call Vinod. Your uncle Chetan has an old story about that. Sit. When I was fifteen, I thought Vinod had forgotten my birthday. I said nothing. I stopped answering his notes, moved to the back bench and took the other road home. I told myself, if he cares, he will ask. He did ask, once, and I looked at my shoes. Vinod decided I was angry about the science project partner he had picked, which was not it at all. He stopped asking. By Diwali we nodded in the corridor like strangers, and the weeks turned into a habit. Last year, forty years on, I met Vinod at a wedding, and he still believed it was about the science project. I never told him about the birthday.

qa.q: Where did Chetan sit after he stopped answering Vinod's notes?
qa.a: Chetan moved to the back bench.

qa.q: What did Chetan hope for by staying silent, and what feeling sat behind it?
qa.a: Chetan hoped Vinod would notice and ask, feeling hurt and proud about the birthday he thought had been forgotten.

qa.q: What could the young Chetan have done when Vinod asked, and why?
qa.a: Chetan could have said that the birthday hurt, because one honest sentence would have replaced Vinod's wrong guess about the science project.

qa.q: How did Vinod read Chetan's silence?
qa.a: Vinod read it as rejection and guessed it was about the science project partner, so Vinod stopped asking and the distance hardened.

grounding: The student stops replying and sits elsewhere hoping the problem disappears, the friend takes it as rejection and guesses the cause wrongly, and the distance hardens over weeks.

subtype: Approach: perspective-taking about the friend's motives [Thinking]
passage:
Manjula: can I say something without you getting upset?
Payal: ok..?
Manjula: I found out Aarti knows about my dance audition fear. I only told you.
Payal: oh no. I did say it to her
Manjula: yeah. I was planning to go silent on you for a week
Payal: fair
Manjula: then I thought, maybe you told her because you were worried, or you just didn't think. Not to hurt me
Payal: I was worried. She asked why you looked pale and I blurted it. I'm sorry 🥺
Manjula: thank you. But if I tell you something private, it stays with you. That part matters to me
Payal: promise. can I fix it with samosas tomorrow 🙂

qa.q: Who did Payal tell about the dance audition fear?
qa.a: Payal told Aarti.

qa.q: What does Manjula think about why Payal told Aarti, and how does it change Manjula's feeling?
qa.a: Manjula thinks Payal was worried or careless rather than malicious, so the hurt gives way to a willingness to ask instead of punish.

qa.q: What could Manjula do if a private thing were shared again, and why?
qa.a: Manjula could share less private news for a while and restate the boundary calmly, because that protects trust without punishing.

qa.q: How might Payal feel on getting Manjula's first message?
qa.a: Payal likely feels nervous and guilty, then relieved that it is a question and not an attack, as the apology and promise show. 🙂

grounding: The student considers that the friend may have told others out of worry or carelessness rather than malice, which shifts the plan from punishment to asking while still stating the boundary.

passage: Kavitha and I sat on the terrace with two cups of tea and agreed on one rule: private things stay private. We wrote it on a page, both of us, like a tiny contract. Then Kavitha went to Naveen and apologised for repeating that Naveen's scholarship form had been rejected. I had let it slip to Kavitha in the first place, so I said I'd been careless too. And then, this was Kavitha's idea, we planned Saturday: cycle to the lake, a flask, no phones. It felt a bit stiff at first. By the second hour we were laughing about the old teacher's whistle again. I'm Saurabh, and honestly, the rule and the ride together fixed more than a long argument would have.

qa.q: What rule did Saurabh and Kavitha agree on?
qa.a: They agreed that private things stay private.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel about the repair plan?
qa.a: Saurabh felt relieved and hopeful, because both had their needs met: a clear rule and time together to rebuild ease. 😊

qa.q: What could Saurabh and Kavitha do if the rule were broken again, and why?
qa.a: They could talk early and openly, before it hardens, and review the rule together, because a repair that both shaped is easier to return to.

qa.q: How might Naveen see Kavitha's apology?
qa.a: Naveen likely feels respected and relieved that Kavitha owned the mistake instead of excusing it.

grounding: Both friends agree that private things stay private, the friend apologises to the affected person, and they plan a shared weekend activity so both needs are met.

subtype: Approach: seeking advice from an older sibling [Action]
passage: Preeti found her brother Jagdish at the far table of the school canteen, where the Class 12 boys ate. "Five minutes," she said. She told it fast: Reema had repeated the name of a boy Preeti liked to the whole bench, and Preeti never wanted to speak to her again. Jagdish chewed slowly. "When did you last reply to her?" "That's not the point." "Preeti." A pause. "Last Tuesday," she admitted. "She sent three messages after that." Jagdish nodded. "I did this to Vikram in ninth. I went quiet, he blurted my business to prove he mattered, and we both lost a term." It stung, but Preeti knew it was fair. "So I talk to her first?" "Say what hurt. And say you went quiet too."

qa.q: Where did Preeti find Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti found Jagdish at the far table of the school canteen.

qa.q: How does Preeti feel on hearing that her silence may have played a part?
qa.a: Preeti feels stung but accepts it, because she knows Jagdish's point is fair.

qa.q: What approach could Preeti take with Reema, and why?
qa.a: Preeti could ask for a quiet chat, say what hurt and admit she went quiet too, because that opens listening on both sides.

qa.q: How might Reema have felt when her messages went unanswered?
qa.a: Reema may have felt dropped and ignored, hurt enough to lash out by repeating the name.

grounding: The student explains the situation to her elder brother, who has been through similar fights, and gets a reality check that helps her see her own part in the misunderstanding.

passage: Picture my birthday guest list: forty names and one gap. That gap was Ritu, after the joke about my haircut in front of the whole class. For a week I ran the plan in my head, and it felt fantastic. I could see the invitation going round and Ritu standing there, not on it. Then I remembered what Ritu told me last year: "When people get annoyed with me, they just stop including me." Ritu was afraid of exactly this. If I did it, I would not be teaching anything; I would be handing over proof. And I would lose the one person who still laughs at my worst jokes. The daydream stayed sweet only as long as I did not think about Ritu's face. I'm Deepak, and I nearly typed that list.

qa.q: How many names were on Deepak's birthday guest list?
qa.a: The guest list had forty names and one gap.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling while running the plan in mind for a week, and what changed?
qa.a: Deepak felt satisfied and vengeful at first, but the feeling soured when Deepak remembered Ritu's fear of being left out.

qa.q: What alternative could Deepak try instead of leaving Ritu out, and why?
qa.a: Deepak could tell Ritu privately that the haircut joke hurt and invite Ritu anyway, because it addresses the hurt without confirming Ritu's fear.

qa.q: How would Ritu see being left off the list?
qa.a: Ritu would likely feel that the fear of being dropped when someone is annoyed had come true, and might pull away from Deepak.

grounding: The student plans to leave the friend out of a birthday party to hurt back, which feels satisfying in imagination but would prove the friend's fear right and cost a friendship worth keeping.

subtype: Approach: noticing the first talk failed and trying a different way [Revision]
passage:
Hansa: You told Megha about my scholarship form!
Ira: Because you never tell me anything!
Hansa: Forget it. Just forget it.
(Next morning, a message on Ira's phone.)
Hansa: That went badly. Can we walk by the lake after school? No shouting, promise 🙂
Ira: ok
(By the lake, evening.)
Hansa: I'm sorry I yelled. I was hurt, that's all.
Ira: I was scared you didn't trust me. And I shouldn't have told Megha.
Hansa: Next time ask me first?
Ira: Yes. Can we sit on the wall for a bit? I brought the biscuits you like.

qa.q: Where did Hansa suggest they walk?
qa.a: Hansa suggested a walk by the lake after school.

qa.q: What does the message 'That went badly' suggest about how Hansa feels?
qa.a: Hansa feels regretful and hopeful about repairing things, shown by the calm tone and the offer of a walk.

qa.q: What else could Hansa try if Ira had not agreed to walk, and why?
qa.a: Hansa could give Ira a few days and write a longer note, because a break can cool tempers and a note lets Ira reply in private.

qa.q: How does Ira see the calm message after the shouting?
qa.a: Ira likely feels relief, having been scared of losing the friendship, so Ira agrees and apologises too. 🤍

grounding: When the face-to-face talk turns into shouting, the student sends a short calm message the next day suggesting a walk, so a change of setting and tone reopens the discussion.

subtype: Approach: accepting that the friendship is changing [Revision]
passage: Zeenat had promised to come to the district quiz final, and Gaurav waited at the school gate until the last auto had left. It was the third promise in two months. The next morning Zeenat said sorry, and seemed to mean it. Gaurav said it was fine, and noticed he had stopped saving a seat. Over the following weeks he sat with Farhan and Disha from the quiz club, went to football on Saturdays, and kept the small things with Zeenat: a hello at the lockers, a joke on the way to the lab. He did not make a speech or keep a score. It felt like a door closing quietly, a little sad, and oddly lighter.

qa.q: How many promises had Zeenat broken by the quiz final?
qa.a: The quiz final was the third promise in two months.

qa.q: What is Gaurav feeling as he stops saving a seat?
qa.a: Gaurav feels a little sad but lighter, since he has stopped waiting for closeness that did not come back.

qa.q: What other approach could Gaurav use if he wanted to try rebuilding?
qa.a: Gaurav could say calmly that kept promises matter to him and ask Zeenat for one small promise to keep, because one honest test shows if trust can return.

qa.q: How might Zeenat notice this change?
qa.a: Zeenat may feel puzzled or hurt by the growing distance, since there is no fight or blame to explain it.

grounding: After repeated broken promises the student sees trust has not returned, keeps a polite connection, invests in other friends and lets the closeness settle lower without blame.

subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of a low-pressure invitation [Thinking]
passage: Thursday, 10 pm. Rehearsal night. I am NOT asking tomorrow in a panic, I am asking with words I already know. Plan: after class, at the lockers, when other people are walking past so it isn't a big scene. "A few of us are doing chemistry practical prep at the library on Saturday. Want to come?" Easy to say no to. If Nikita says yes: "Great, we start at three." If no: "No worries, another time." Practised in the mirror three times and my voice wobbled on "want to come," so I practised that bit slowly. If it goes badly I will survive. I already know what I'd say either way. 🙂 - Aditi

qa.q: Where does Aditi plan to ask Nikita?
qa.a: Aditi plans to ask at the lockers after class, when other people are walking past.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling while rehearsing in the mirror?
qa.a: Aditi was nervous but determined; the wobbly voice on 'want to come' shows the nerves, and the extra slow practice shows the resolve.

qa.q: What could Aditi do if Nikita says no, and why?
qa.a: Aditi could keep chatting about shared subjects and not ask again soon, because giving space keeps things easy and comfortable.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel receiving the invitation?
qa.a: Nikita would likely feel at ease, since a group study session is easy to decline and there is no pressure to answer in a particular way.

grounding: The student imagines asking a classmate to a group study session, picks words that are easy to decline, and prepares a calm reply for either answer.

subtype: Approach: building a friendly connection first [Action]
passage: Three weeks before the inter-house fest, Damini and Abhinav ended up on the same poster team. The art room was loud, with drums being tested next door, so most of their talking happened over paint trays. Damini asked what he listened to while painting, and next day brought a link to a song she thought he'd like. He laughed easily when the club was around, but went short when a question got personal, so she kept to posters, robotics club and the fest schedule. In the third week, with two days left, she said to the group, "A few of us are getting samosas after the last rehearsal. Come along?" Abhinav grinned. "Sure, if Rehan is coming too."

qa.q: How long before the inter-house fest did Damini and Abhinav join the poster team?
qa.a: They joined the poster team three weeks before the fest.

qa.q: What does Damini think about how comfortable Abhinav feels, and what does Damini want to avoid?
qa.a: Damini thinks Abhinav is uneasy when questions get personal, and wants to avoid pressure, so Damini keeps talk to posters, robotics club and the fest schedule.

qa.q: What alternative could Damini try if Abhinav seemed uneasy even with a group plan, and why?
qa.a: Damini could keep the friendship on projects and let Abhinav lead any next step, because comfort matters more than a quick answer.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Damini's group invitation?
qa.a: Abhinav probably finds it relaxed and easy to accept, especially with Rehan there, so it feels like an invitation to friends and not pressure.

grounding: Over a few weeks the student chats about shared interests in projects and clubs, watching whether the other person is comfortable, before suggesting a casual group activity.
